video_title: How to build a more flexible, quieter, less obnoxious data center
gist: Varys CEO Nelson Abramson, a two-decade Google data center veteran, tells David Roberts how his Sidewalk Infrastructure Partners-backed startup replaces diesel generators with large LFP battery arrays, evaporative cooling towers with air-cooled chillers, and low-voltage distribution with a medium-voltage power plane — claiming up to 77% utilization of provisioned utility capacity versus ~49% conventionally. He also defends the company's noise, water and by-right-industrial-land claims for its stalled Lyon Township (Michigan) and Salem (Oregon) projects, where the Oregon governor pulled a public land sale and recall petitions were launched against council members who approved the Michigan site.

insights.claim: Varys CEO Nelson Abramson argues that at 500 MW to 1 GW campus scale a data center should be underwritten as an energy asset rather than as industrial real estate, which is the framing that opens up power-side design innovation.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Investors screening data center developers should test whether a sponsor prices grid interconnection and storage as the core asset, not square footage, since that determines margin per interconnect.
insights.quote: It's really an energy asset that happens to consume real estate.

insights.claim: Abramson frames data centers as conversion engines from utility capacity into compute capacity, making any gain in compute-per-provisioned-watt a first-order value driver because utilities can only deliver so many watts per location.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: In a grid-constrained buildout, efficiency of the interconnect — not land or shell cost — becomes the scarce input that sets developer returns.

insights.claim: Data center capacity has scaled 50–100x over roughly 30 years — from Abramson's first sub-1 MW site in a converted Hechinger's hardware store to next-generation Nvidia racks at over a megawatt each — while the core electrical and mechanical design template stayed essentially unchanged.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A design template that scaled by replication rather than redesign is the opening Varys is attacking; incumbents carrying that template may face a cost-per-compute disadvantage.
insights.quote: The next generation Nvidia racks are going to be a megawatt plus each per rack.

insights.claim: Varys has not yet built an operating data center; it runs a pre-production environment at its Bay Area headquarters and has spent roughly 18 months on a full-scale lab test bed with a national lab plus MISO and Xcel, modeling utility interactions and ride-through of recent PJM disturbances.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Execution risk is still binary — none of the efficiency claims have been demonstrated in a commercial facility, so the lab and utility partnerships are the only third-party validation available today.

insights.claim: Abramson concedes every Varys component is separately purchasable — Emerald AI for compute capping, a vendor he names as On Energy for battery backup, and the medium-voltage approach from a 2020 Google paper — and argues the existence of those vendors should increase confidence the claims are real.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Component availability means the moat is integration and operations, not intellectual property — a weaker barrier to entry than it first appears.

insights.claim: Abramson's case for integration rests on cross-component trade-offs and pooling, plus the argument that telemetry, optimization and ongoing operation — not construction — are what actually deliver the promised efficiency gains.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Shifts the diligence question from hardware specs to operating capability, which is harder to verify pre-construction.

insights.claim: Abramson adds contractual risk transfer as a fourth pillar of the pitch: a single counterparty signs up for the efficiency, operating points and SLA rather than five vendors pointing fingers at each other.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The business model itself — one throat to choke on performance guarantees — may be as important to winning leases as the technology.

insights.claim: Conventional data centers step utility voltage down to low voltage early and distribute from there, which wastes copper and aluminum and incurs heat losses; Varys keeps power at medium voltage across a shared power plane and converts only at the last mile near the rack.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Less conductor per megawatt is a direct capex lever and a hedge against copper price inflation across the AI buildout.

insights.claim: Early low-voltage conversion forces conventional designs to bucketize capacity into roughly 500 kW to 2 MW blocks that cannot be reclaimed once allocated, so capacity planners are stranded with unusable slack rather than deploying against the full 50–100 MW campus number.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Stranded power inside existing facilities is a quantifiable inefficiency that retrofit or new-build vendors can monetize.

insights.claim: Sharing power campus-wide via the medium-voltage plane lets Varys fit roughly a third more racks into the same underlying data center capacity, by exploiting the statistical fact that a meaningful fraction of servers are idle at any moment.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A third more racks per interconnect is the central economic claim to diligence; if real it changes revenue per megawatt of scarce grid capacity.
insights.quote: we're able to get something like a third more racks into the same underlying data center capacity

insights.claim: Varys claims it can use up to 77% of provisioned utility capacity versus roughly 49% for a conventional design, which Abramson pitches as effectively getting a fourth data center free for every three leased.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: This is the headline number a lease counterparty or investor should stress-test, since both figures are modeled rather than measured in a commercial facility.
insights.quote: you lease three various data centers, you get the fourth for free

insights.claim: Varys replaces the diesel generator fleet that is the hallmark of conventional data centers with large LFP battery arrays of the same type utilities and IPPs already deploy for grid storage, using them as primary backup at the proposed Detroit-area project.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Grid-scale battery demand gains a new customer class if data center backup shifts from diesel to LFP, with knock-on volume for stationary storage suppliers.

insights.claim: Conventional UPS systems use rooms of lead-acid batteries sized for about five minutes of runtime that must pick up load in under 1/60th of a second, and that sub-cycle requirement is precisely what forces early low-voltage conversion and power bucketization.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific design constraint that a battery-energy-storage architecture removes, which is the mechanism behind the claimed utilization gain.

insights.claim: The industry has moved sub-second ride-through duty from centralized UPS rooms to small batteries on each server, which is more energy efficient despite requiring 10,000 batteries instead of 100 because it eliminates two full AC/DC conversion steps and their heat losses.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive case where unit-cost inefficiency wins on total energy efficiency — the same logic that could later justify DC distribution.
insights.quote: a room full of car batteries is actually less efficient of an implementation than putting a little battery on every server

insights.claim: Abramson believes batteries, inverters and power control systems are improving fast enough that a single large battery could soon handle both sub-cycle smoothing and long-duration backup, though he doubts end users would trust it or bother removing rack-level batteries from ultra-dense GPU/TPU systems.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Watch inverter and power-electronics vendors: collapsing two battery layers into one would remove cost from every rack.

insights.claim: Despite the no-diesel branding, Varys' Michigan filings include small kilowatt-to-100-kilowatt-scale diesel generators mandated by fire code for sprinkler pumps and life safety, while the Salem, Oregon plan does include conventional diesel generators because customers wanted the optionality.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The diesel-free claim is customer-dependent, so marketing and filings can diverge — a diligence item for anyone underwriting the emissions story.

insights.claim: Abramson says different tenant workloads carry different backup risk appetites — generalized cloud, training, inference and market trading algorithms each take a different view — so firm generation at a site is often about customer optionality rather than engineering necessity.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Backup capex per site is set by the tenant's risk profile, which means the same developer's projects will not have uniform emissions or cost profiles.

insights.claim: Varys sizes backup at a nominal four hours measured against a worst-case design day — the hottest, most humid day of the past 50 years with the facility 100% full and every server at 100% — so real-world runtime is meaningfully longer than four hours.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The four-hour figure is a floor under stacked worst cases, not an expected value — relevant to anyone modeling curtailment risk for tenants.

insights.claim: Four hours was chosen because utility demand response and capacity markets are structured in two-to-four-hour strips, which Abramson says can be verified directly in RTO program design rather than taken on faith.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Battery duration in data centers is being set by capacity-market product design, so changes to RTO strip length would reset the hardware spec across the sector.

insights.claim: Abramson rebuts the multi-day heat dome objection by noting grids are constrained only for part of each day — California is a solar exporter from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and peaks 4 to 8 p.m. before wind picks up around 8 or 9 p.m. — leaving unconstrained hours in which to recharge.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Duration adequacy depends on the diurnal shape of scarcity, not total event length, which is the same logic that underpins four-hour grid storage economics generally.

insights.claim: To make four-hour backup work as a firm capacity product, Varys must contract for enough spare non-firm interconnect capacity and electrical headroom to recharge the batteries during unconstrained hours, which becomes part of the negotiation with the utility.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Recharge headroom is a hidden requirement that could limit where this model works, since it needs interconnects with slack rather than fully subscribed ones.

insights.claim: Abramson argues it is bad capital allocation to use servers as a virtual battery, since buying more hours of storage is far cheaper than buying multiples of server capacity to idle during grid events.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to compute-curtailment-first flexibility vendors: the cost comparison decides whether storage or compute throttling becomes the industry default.
insights.quote: If we need 12 hours, we can install 12 hours of battery for a lot cheaper than 3x numbers of servers.

insights.claim: Abramson says published regulatory utility outage data shows four hours exceeds what is needed for outage coverage, and dismisses the 48-hour scenario by noting that a 230 kV system down for two days would be a level of disruption where phone service is not the top concern.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Sets the practical ceiling on backup duration demand, capping the addressable market for very-long-duration and non-combustion backup at data centers.

insights.claim: Abramson sees promising non-combustion long-duration options — fuel cells, linear engines such as Mainspring's, and chemistries where the energy storage medium is swapped in real time like a consumable fuel — but argues the outage data strongly says data centers do not need them.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for long-duration backup vendors targeting data centers as their beachhead market.

insights.claim: Priority-aware capping at Varys is a tenant-executed function: Varys supplies energy storage management, consumption visibility and outage telemetry, and the customer decides which compute layers get dialed down.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Splits the flexibility stack into an infrastructure layer and a scheduler layer, defining where a landlord's product ends and a software vendor's begins.

insights.claim: Abramson contradicts the common assumption that most compute is firm, arguing every large system carries an enormous volume of deferrable batch processing plus tunable knobs inside supposedly live queries — index depth, longtail search, cross-posting, third-party pushes, ad density — so the floor for a live service is well below 100% but not zero.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: If live user-facing compute is far more elastic than assumed, the flexible-load resource available to grids is much larger than headline estimates.
insights.quote: There's all of these different levers that can get pulled.

insights.claim: Because no one runs large-scale systems without redundancy, operators can declare a data center unreliable and redirect demand to another site at a cost of only 10 to 20 milliseconds of added latency, making geographic load shifting a practical flexibility lever.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Spatial load shifting between regions is nearly free in user-experience terms, which matters for how much demand response a single grid can actually call on.

insights.claim: Abramson says priority-aware capping is a value add-on rather than a leasing requirement, because essentially every large compute operator already runs internal priority layers to hit reasonable average utilization — so it does not narrow the pool of eligible tenants.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Removes a commonly cited leasing objection to flexible data centers: the tenant capability already exists in-house.
insights.quote: It is not a requirement. It is a value add-on.

insights.claim: Pressed on what Emerald AI adds if hyperscalers already cap their own compute, Abramson says the remaining opportunity is better scheduler management and making power an explicit scheduling constraint rather than the capping capability itself.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Narrows the defensible value proposition for compute-flexibility software to scheduler optimization, not basic load curtailment.

insights.claim: Varys swaps evaporative cooling towers for air-cooled chillers, which it says cuts water use 95–99% versus a conventional data center but trades water for fan noise, mitigated with oversized slow-running fans, sound baffles, berms and landscaping.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Names the explicit water-for-noise trade in closed-loop cooling, which is the axis on which every siting fight over these designs will be argued.

insights.claim: Abramson reconciles the water numbers by explaining that on an average day site water goes only to bathrooms and landscaping, while the adiabatic system runs only five to ten days a year in a worst case — and that burst accounts for the bulk of the multi-million-gallon annual figure.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Annual water totals for these designs are dominated by a handful of peak days, so headline gallon counts overstate routine draw on local supply.

insights.claim: Roberts flags that Varys told Lyon Township in a December 2025 presentation it would use 15,000 gallons annually while July 2026 materials put annual usage under 12 million gallons; Abramson says he does not recall the 15,000 figure and insists the company's numbers have been consistent, refined as design details firmed up.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: An unresolved three-orders-of-magnitude discrepancy in public filings is exactly the kind of credibility gap that fuels local opposition and permitting delay.

insights.claim: Abramson contextualizes 12 million gallons a year as roughly three Cheesecake Factories, and dramatically less water acre-for-acre than agriculture or a golf course.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The comparison framing developers use publicly is itself a signal of how contested the water narrative has become in data center siting.

insights.claim: No independently verified sound study exists for either project: Salem's has not been done because equipment selection and site plan are not far enough along, and the Lyon Township study was redone to the township consultants' preferred methodology after technical disputes.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The quiet-data-center claim is currently unverified at both sites, leaving permitting timelines exposed to acoustic review outcomes.

insights.claim: Abramson says Varys' Michigan modeling puts sound at roughly library level at the property line, well below what local ordinance allows, and commits to monitoring its own sound against limits agreed with the municipality.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A falsifiable, enforceable commitment that communities and counterparties can hold the developer to once a facility operates.
insights.quote: in the neighborhood of a library level sound at the property line which is well below what is actually allowed by ordinance

insights.claim: Abramson says he is open to third-party monitoring and public reporting of noise and water, noting water is already third-party metered by the water company, and that as a resident he would want assurances, validation and enforcement.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Verified monitoring commitments may become the price of entry for data center permits, adding a compliance cost line to project models.

insights.claim: Varys deliberately targets land already zoned industrial and buildable by right rather than rezoning agricultural land, because Abramson says rezoning farmland has been extremely controversial across his three decades in siting regardless of what was being built.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Land strategy is now a primary determinant of data center schedule risk, and by-right inventory is the scarce resource developers are racing for.

insights.claim: The Lyon Township parcel has been designated industrial since at least 1957 and was once planned as a Chrysler engine factory, which Abramson uses as evidence the community itself long ago chose that site for industrial development.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Decades of industrial designation did not prevent opposition, showing that legal entitlement no longer guarantees social license.

insights.claim: Roberts notes opponents argue Lyon Township's ordinance requires public review for any industrial facility over 100,000 square feet, and challenges Varys that targeting land where public approval can be avoided is a poor look for a self-described good neighbor.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: A live legal question over whether by-right status actually holds at this site is a concrete threat to the project's timeline.

insights.claim: Varys is offering Lyon Township a $10 million community benefits package — $5 million for infrastructure and resiliency, $2 million for public safety, $3 million for education and workforce — plus 210 permanent jobs and roughly $300 million in property taxes over 17 years, in a community of about 28,000 people.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: Benchmarks the going rate for data center community benefits, and shows that even very large per-resident payments are not clearing local opposition.

insights.claim: Recall petitions were launched against every Lyon Township council member who approved the by-right project, which Roberts reads as evidence that data center opposition has detached from concrete concerns and become an unsatisfiable public panic.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: If no concession package can buy consent, siting risk becomes a structural discount on data center development everywhere, not a project-level variable.

insights.claim: After Oregon's governor cancelled the public land sale in July, Varys filed through a subsidiary to buy private land in Salem and advanced a permit; Abramson disputes that Salem has a moratorium, saying the council only passed a motion to examine one and could take another 30 days to actually adopt it.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The Oregon project's entitlement status is live and contested, and the subsidiary-purchase maneuver is the kind of optics that hardens local resistance.

insights.claim: Abramson says the Salem site is former prison land inside an official industrial park and enterprise zone for at least 20 years, bordered by a municipal airport, a prison and three warehouses, and that the completed project would raise Salem's property tax base by roughly one third.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: A one-third increase in a city's tax base quantifies how large the fiscal prize is, and how much municipalities stand to lose by blocking projects.

insights.claim: Data centers tripping to backup power during grid fluctuations has already dropped hundreds of megawatts to a gigawatt of demand at once across multiple sites, creating real grid stability events rather than theoretical risk.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: This observed failure mode is the regulatory trigger behind mandatory ride-through, which will impose retrofit costs across the existing fleet.

insights.claim: Texas made ride-through mandatory as of October 1 and FERC has NERC drafting standards that could make it universal, a rulemaking Varys has actively supported by filing comments and working with NERC on the standards.
insights.speaker: David Roberts
insights.so_what: A compliance deadline that converts a design advantage into a legal requirement — favorable near-term for vendors already compliant, and a cost shock for those not.

insights.claim: Abramson argues gigawatt-scale data centers must be planned as extensions of the grid because a swing of that size is inherently destructive, making ride-through non-optional for anyone connecting hundreds of megawatts.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Reframes large loads as grid assets subject to reliability obligations, foreshadowing more interconnection conditions on data center developers.
insights.quote: it is clear the largecale data centers have to be planned as though they are extensions of the grid

insights.claim: Asked whether mandatory ride-through erodes his competitive moat, Abramson says he welcomes losing it because universal adoption is the point, and puts the burden on his team to make a more impressive V2 design.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Concedes the current architecture is not a durable moat, so valuation should rest on execution speed and land position rather than defensible technology.
insights.quote: I look forward to having no competitive mode because everybody has copied us because it's amazing.

insights.claim: Abramson expects the next wave of innovation to come from technologies that only make sense at gigawatt scale — batteries, transformers, superconductors and cooling — noting that a single rack drawing a megawatt changes what energy distribution even means.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Scale itself unlocks new supplier categories, so component vendors priced for 10–100 MW facilities may be mispricing the gigawatt-era opportunity.

insights.claim: Abramson sees high-voltage DC distribution as a real opportunity for eliminating DC/AC conversion losses but flags new problems around disconnects and segmentation because transformers cannot be used, framing it as possibly a race between DC and superconductors.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: Two competing paths to the same efficiency prize; whichever wins reshapes the supply chain for data center electrical equipment.
insights.quote: maybe there's a race between DC and superconductors

insights.claim: Abramson names the missing communication pathway between utility, data center, compute user and compute scheduler as a major industry gap and a very active area of Varys investment — a software problem he finds more surprising than the power-side ones.
insights.speaker: Nelson Abramson
insights.so_what: The interface layer between grid signals and compute schedulers is an unbuilt software market that both Varys and flexibility vendors are moving toward.
